Russian ballistic missile strikes hit three major bridges across Kyiv’s Dnipro River on Friday, killing three people and injuring 15, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. 
The attacks forced bridge closures and traffic restrictions, damaged critical infrastructure and sparked fires. 
The strikes followed Putin’s warning of retaliation after Ukraine attacked the Crimean Bridge for a third time this week. 
Apartment buildings in Dnipropetrovsk, a hospital in Kharkiv and a tram in Zaporizhzhia were also struck, local officials said.

🔊 FBI Director says US tech outages are inevitable — blames previous administrations
FBI Director Kash Patel is addressing the catastrophic string of nationwide system failures by claiming that "technical disruptions" are simply unavoidable, while pointing the finger at the previous administration for leaving behind "legacy" systems.
💬 "There will be some technical disruptions like what we've seen... Legacy meaning other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn't. We are. We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time."
It has taken the current administration nearly two years to even begin updating the nation's critical infrastructure. The timing is brutally ironic: they finally start patching the network, and the entire country's banking and aviation systems immediately crash.
The FAA grounded thousands of flights because of a router bought in 2001. Banks froze because of ancient backend systems. Yet, instead of taking responsibility for a crumbling domestic grid, Patel is deflecting to the private sector and vowing to "hunt down nefarious actors" all over the world.

🤝 Iraq reaches deal with Kataib Hezbollah — without the US
Iraq’s government has reached a last-minute agreement with Kataib Hezbollah instead of forcing the militia out of a key town south of Baghdad it has controlled since 2014, according to Al Jazeera.
🔴 Officials had accused the group of stealing hundreds of millions in state oil.
🔴 Facing threats of armed resistance and intervention by Iran’s Quds Force commander, Baghdad opted for a compromise rather than a confrontation.
🔴 The deal establishes a shared security presence starting tomorrow afternoon, mixing army, police, and militia fighters under a new command.
Iraqi government didn't get a total military victory—the militia keeps its role. But Iraq proved a much larger point: it is capable of managing its own complex web of factions and security challenges through internal consensus and regional diplomacy, without US interference.
